intent: Keep the iteration 4 layout (5 sensors at y=0.07 m, 16 mm footprint, track 0.10 m, radius 0.040 m) and reduce mass from 0.6 to 0.5 kg. The aim is lower yaw inertia so the robot tracks s-bend and slalom curvature without losing the line. This is a single-variable test against iteration 4. Expected: s-bend and slalom max_error falls below 0.06 m and line_loss_events drops, while the oval finish rate stays at 80% or higher.
learning: Hypotheses: (1) Mass 0.5 kg reduces s-bend and slalom max_error relative to iteration 4 because yaw inertia drops. (2) Oval completion stays at or above 80%, since the speed gain from radius 0.040 m is unchanged. (3) If steering_oscillation rises while max_error does not move, the bottleneck is controller gain, not geometry, and the Integrator should be told so. (4) If max_error still reaches 0.06 m on the bends with few line losses, the next lever is wheel_track (narrower for more turn authority) rather than more sensing or mass.
rationale: Iteration 4 is the best design so far (372.6). Its only change from iteration 2 was wheel radius 0.035 to 0.040 m. The oval finish rate rose from 65% to 80%, mean completion time fell to 1.875 s, and oval progress reached 0.97. The s-bend and slalom still end at the 0.06 m off-track limit with progress of 0.57 and 0.14. Their max_error sits at the limit, and s-bend steering_oscillation is high at 0.32. Earlier results show that spread alone (iteration 1) and extra look-ahead with seven sensors (iteration 3) did not help. The sensor layout is therefore kept at the iteration 4 values, which is the best-supported configuration. The remaining bottleneck on the bends looks like inertia and lag: the robot cannot turn fast enough once the line drifts. Yaw inertia is mass*(L^2+W^2)/12, so reducing mass from 0.6 to 0.5 kg lowers the turning inertia by about 17% with no change to sensing. Expected result: a smaller max_error and a higher s-bend progress, with the oval finish rate held at 80% or better. I am changing one variable, so any shift in results can be attributed to mass.
